```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 9.5,
                     fig.height = 5, dpi = 110)
library(SimSurvey)
vignette_widget <- function(p) {
  p <- plotly::partial_bundle(p, type = "cartesian", local = FALSE)
  axes <- grep("^[xy]axis[0-9]*$", names(p$x$layout), value = TRUE)
  for (axis in axes) p$x$layout[[axis]]$automargin <- TRUE
  margins <- list(l = 80, r = 45, t = 50, b = 85)
  if (!is.null(p$x$layout$legend$y) && p$x$layout$legend$y < 0) margins$b <- 140
  p$x$layout$margin <- margins
  index <- which(vapply(p$dependencies,
    function(dependency) dependency$name == "plotly-cartesian", logical(1)))
  # Keep only the large Plotly bundle external; embed local support resources.
  p$dependencies[[index]]$script <- list(list(
    src = p$dependencies[[index]]$script, "data-external" = "1"))
  p
}
```

## Questions the new features can answer

SimSurvey now supports multiple fisheries with user-supplied allocations, their reporting and biological
monitoring, and multiple survey programs observing the same population. Weight
and maturity relationships also provide biomass and mature-biomass truth. These
are extensions to the framework described by
[Regular et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0232822); that paper
provides the background on population generation and stratified survey analysis.
This vignette describes the extensions in development version 0.1.8.9000, toward
0.2.0, rather than repeating those established methods.

| Question | New capability |
|:---|:---|
| How are user-supplied fishery allocations realized? | Interleaved operations share stocks and mortality budgets. |
| How do targeting and imperfect knowledge affect effort and CPUE? | Separate controls for targeting, knowledge error, and exploration. |
| How do biological relationships and gear selection affect the quantities observed? | Shared weight and maturity models; age- or length-based selectivity. |
| How do reporting and monitoring affect the available data? | Reporting errors, preferential coverage, and nested biological observations. |
| How do different survey programs observe one population? | Independent programs with distinct settings and a standard extraction interface. |

The model is **conditional on the generated population and total mortality**.
Fishing allocates deaths permitted by `Z`; effort determines how catches are
obtained. This is useful for examining data-generation and sampling mechanisms.
It does not turn SimSurvey into a population-feedback or management-strategy model.
The interactive figures use the package's Plotly graphics. Viewing them requires
access to the shared Plotly web asset; building this vignette does not download it.

```{r workflow, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.3, fig.cap="Data flow. Both fisheries and surveys start from the annual population snapshot. Survey programs do not sample the stock left behind by the fisheries."}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 1.04), ylim = c(0, 1))
box_text <- function(x, y, label) {
  rect(x - 0.14, y - 0.14, x + 0.14, y + 0.14,
       col = "#EDF3F7", border = "#52758C")
  text(x, y, label, cex = 0.8)
}
box_text(0.17, 0.74, "Annual population\nN, Z, growth")
box_text(0.52, 0.74, "Shared fisheries\nCatches and effort")
box_text(0.87, 0.74, "Reporting\nBiological samples")
box_text(0.17, 0.24, "Weight and maturity\nBiomass B, mature B: S")
box_text(0.52, 0.24, "Independent\nsurvey programs")
box_text(0.87, 0.24, "Select one survey\nExisting analyses")
arrows(c(0.31, 0.66, 0.17, 0.31, 0.66), c(0.74, 0.74, 0.60, 0.64, 0.24),
       c(0.38, 0.73, 0.17, 0.38, 0.73), c(0.74, 0.74, 0.38, 0.34, 0.24),
       length = 0.07, col = "#52758C")
```

## Shared biological truth

All examples use one synthetic groundfish population over **2001--2005**.
The setup follows the example in `sim_survey()`: five ages, a 20-km grid, and
default population and spatial processes. We use calendar-year labels for
readability. Recruitment, mortality, growth, weight, maturity, depth associations,
and age-year-space variation all use their defaults. No trend, fixed core, or
cell-specific population share is prescribed. This is an illustrative stochastic
population, not a calibrated reconstruction of 3Ps cod.

```{r population}
set.seed(601)
population <- sim_abundance(ages = 1:5, years = 2001:2005) |>
  sim_distribution(grid = make_grid(res = c(20, 20)))
```

`sim_abundance()` now retains three biological relationships. `sim_growth()` is
an alias for `sim_vonB()`; its returned function remains stored as `sim_length`.
`sim_weight()` provides kilograms given length in centimetres. `sim_maturity()`
provides maturity probability, by length by default. Supply alternatives through
the `growth`, `weight`, and `maturity` arguments. For example,
`maturity = sim_maturity(x50 = 50)` changes the midpoint while retaining the other
defaults. Use `maturity_by = "age"` with age-appropriate parameters for an age ogive.

Weight defaults follow the reference relationship used for 3Ps cod in
[Varkey et al. (2024), Table 10](https://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2024/mpo-dfo/Fs97-13-1381-eng.pdf).
Maturity defaults approximate the historical female relationship for 1996 in
[Brattey and Morgan (1996), Table 3](https://waves-vagues.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/Library/198884.pdf).
These defaults are convenient starting points, not contemporary stock-specific
calibrations. One maturity curve applies to all simulated fish.

```{r biology-curves, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.5}
length_cm <- 0:100
weight_curve <- plotly::plot_ly(x = length_cm, y = sim_weight()(length_cm),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Weight") |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Length (cm)"), yaxis = list(title = "Weight (kg)"))
maturity_curve <- plotly::plot_ly(x = length_cm, y = sim_maturity()(length_cm),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Maturity probability") |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Length (cm)"), yaxis = list(title = "Maturity probability"))
plotly::subplot(weight_curve, maturity_curve, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(showlegend = FALSE) |> vignette_widget()
```

The maturity midpoint gives probability 0.5, rather than a minimum size at which
every fish becomes mature.

`B` and `S` are age-by-year matrices of expected biomass and mature biomass in
kilograms. `B_at_length` and `S_at_length` give the corresponding length-by-year
quantities. Spatial `sp_N` also contains expected `B` and `S`. The two
representations have matching annual totals:

```{r biomass}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(colSums(population$B), colSums(population$B_at_length))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(colSums(population$S), colSums(population$S_at_length))))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  year = population$years,
  biomass_tonnes = round(colSums(population$B) / 1000),
  mature_biomass_tonnes = round(colSums(population$S) / 1000)
), row.names = FALSE)
```

The existing trend helper now accepts biological mass matrices:

```{r biomass-trends, fig.height=4.5}
plotly::subplot(plot_trend(population, mat = "B"), plot_trend(population, mat = "S"),
                titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(showlegend = FALSE) |> vignette_widget()
```

Here `S` is mature biomass of **all fish** under the supplied curve, without a
female fraction or a spawning-season adjustment. It does not drive recruitment.
Both mass summaries integrate over the length-age key: weight at mean length is
generally not mean weight, and separately averaging weight and maturity loses
their association. [Appendix A](#appendix-a-mathematics-of-the-extensions) gives
the joint calculation and a numerical example.

## Two fisheries sharing one population

Calling `sim_fishery()` without `sim` constructs a configuration, without
simulating anything or consuming random numbers. All fisheries and their allocations are
declared together. Their names become identifiers in the results.

```{r configurations}
trawl <- sim_fishery(fishery_share = 0.2, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 400))
gillnet <- sim_fishery(
  fishery_share = 0.1, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 200),
  selectivity = sim_logistic(x50 = 40), selectivity_by = "length"
)

set.seed(502)
fished <- population |>
  sim_fisheries(trawl = trawl, gillnet = gillnet, n_sims = 5)
```

The gear names denote illustrative programs, not calibrated gear models. The
trawl configuration uses default age selectivity; the second configuration
demonstrates length selectivity. For a single fishery, supply the population
directly to `sim_fishery(population, ...)` instead.

```{r individual-fishery, eval=FALSE}
population |>
  sim_fishery(fishery_share = 0.2, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 400))
```

`sim_capture()` is a generic encounter model. The symbol `q` is conventional in
[fisheries catch/effort models](https://www.fao.org/4/x5685e/x5685e04.htm).
Its required `q` has grid-area
units per gear-time unit. These coefficients suit the coarse grid and nominal
effort units used here; they are not estimates of actual trawl or gillnet
efficiency. Default `gear_amount` and `duration` are each one. Their product is
effort. Set `gear_unit` and `time_unit` when defining physical units for a real
application. Gear amount and duration can also be operation-level callbacks;
`capacity_per_gear` adds a capacity limit to the encounter model.

**Fishery capture `q` differs from survey `q`**, which is a dimensionless
catchability probability. Capture `q` is a coefficient, can exceed one, and is
converted to a bounded encounter probability internally. The appendix distinguishes
fishery \(q_f\) from survey \(q_{s,l}\). Also, selectivity is not automatically rescaled to a
maximum of one: its magnitude affects the reference target as well as capture.

Each reference target uses the original population, `Z`, the fishery share, and
mean selectivity. A share of 0.2 therefore need not mean 20% of all deaths: mean
selectivity also matters. The engine chooses the next active fishery uniformly
for each operation, depletes shared age-length stocks, and enforces shared
age-specific death budgets. Reference shares must be compatible at every age
and year. They are rejected, rather than normalized, when incompatible.
This is an allocation-based framework, analogous to setting catch allocations
before fishing. Here allocations are shares of mortality before selectivity,
translated into targets in numbers, rather than directly supplied kilogram TACs.

```{r annual}
knitr::kable(fished$fishery$annual[sim == 1,
  list(fishery, year, target, n, shortfall, status)])
ledger <- fished$fishery$mortality_ledger
stopifnot(all(ledger$starting == ledger$fishery_deaths +
                ledger$other_deaths + ledger$survivors))
```

The most useful new outputs are:

| Component in `fishery` | Use |
|:---|:---|
| `annual` | Targets, achieved catches, effort, CPUE, shortfalls, and status |
| `setdet` | Operations, including zero catches, reports, sampling counts, and constraint flags |
| `catch_at_age`, `catch_at_length` | Aggregate true catch composition |
| `sp_removals` | Fishery-specific spatial removals |
| `mortality_ledger` | One shared count balance, not a separate population per fishery |
| `reference` | Reference and realized catches and F at age, original N/Z, and shared `total_deaths` |
| `samp` | Biological observations and sampling-stage probabilities |

All fisheries inherit `population$sim_weight`, so catch kilograms and biomass
CPUE share the population weight relationship. Targets remain in **numbers**.
Fishery stocks and catches remain aggregate. Only bounded biological samples
are expanded into individual records. Use `light = FALSE` to retain joint
age-length catches and sample truth when inspecting a small simulation.

### What does a shortfall mean?

The allocation sets an intended catch; the operations determine what is actually
caught. A **shortfall is the integer target minus realized catch**, in fish.
Shared stocks, access restrictions, and gear responses can constrain an allocation.
The status explains why fishing stopped:

| Status | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| `target_met` | The number target was caught, including a zero target. |
| `exhausted` | No eligible accessible catching opportunities remain; this includes known zero capture or capacity. |
| `operation_limit` | The permitted operations ended while catch remained below target. More operations might help, but are not guaranteed to do so. |

Invalid inputs, including incompatible reference shares, produce errors instead.

For example, with 100 fish, `Z = log(2)`, full selectivity, and share 0.4, there
are 50 expected deaths and a reference target of 20 fish. If access permits only
five catches, the shortfall is 15 fish. The ledger allocates 45 other deaths and
50 survivors. The unused fishing allocation becomes other deaths because total
mortality was fixed upstream. It does not leave an additional 15 survivors or
improve next year's generated population. Other deaths can include mortality
from processes beyond this simulated fishery, not just natural mortality.

The new diagnostics distinguish intended and realized mortality. For this example,
reference F is \(0.4\log(2)\simeq0.277\); realized-equivalent F is
\((5/100)\log(2)/(1-0.5)\simeq0.069\). The removal fraction is 0.05.
These diagnostics are retained at age:

```{r mortality-diagnostics}
knitr::kable(fished$fishery$reference[sim == 1 & year == 2001,
  list(fishery, age, N, total_deaths, catch_reference, catch_realized,
       F_reference = round(F_reference, 3), F_realized = round(F_realized, 3))])
```

`total_deaths` is the **whole-fish count assigned to all mortality** for that
age/year, derived from \(N(1-e^{-Z})\) with balanced rounding across ages.
It includes deaths attributed to all simulated fisheries **plus other deaths**.
It is not one fishery's allocation or its remaining catch allowance. The same
shared value appears on each fishery's reference row; do not sum it across
fisheries. At the end, it equals `fishery_deaths + other_deaths` summed over
cells for that age/year in the mortality ledger. In the 100-fish example it is
50, regardless of whether that fishery catches five or twenty fish.

`F_realized` inverts Baranov using the original `N` and fixed `Z`; it is a
catch-equivalent diagnostic, not an estimated operation-time hazard. The catch
target is a total number, so realized age composition, and therefore F at each
age, may differ even when that target is met. Integer budget rounding can also
produce differences in tiny populations. There is no implicit annual average F.

Interleaving specifies operation order, not calendar time. Other deaths are
allocated after fishing, and subsequent annual populations were generated
before fishing. Thus neither this ledger nor `S` describes seasonal spawning
biomass or persistent spatial depletion carried into the next year.

## How do targeting and knowledge affect effort and CPUE?

The default fishery favors high vulnerable density (`targeting = 1`), has accurate
knowledge (`knowledge_sd = 0`), and allocates 5% of location probability uniformly
to exploration. Zero targeting produces uniform accessible locations. Location
choice uses the **current year's** vulnerable density, updated as catches remove
fish. Positive `knowledge_sd` adds a noisy density map: new cell errors are
drawn each year and persist across that year's operations. Fisheries therefore
respond to shifting distributions, with imperfect knowledge when requested.
This is contemporaneous noisy knowledge, without learning, a lagged map, or
vessel routing. A positive targeting exponent does not guarantee a good choice
in every operation.

We keep the population and the other fishery's allocation fixed. A small helper makes the
controlled changes visible and avoids repeating the full pipeline. Seeding is
explicit caller code; package functions do not reseed themselves.

```{r spatial-comparisons}
run_fleets <- function(trawl_spec) {
  set.seed(502)
  sim_fisheries(population, trawl = trawl_spec, gillnet = gillnet, n_sims = 5)
}
uniform <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl, list(targeting = 0)))
noisy <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl, list(knowledge_sd = 1)))
spatial_scenarios <- list(Uniform = uniform, Targeted = fished, Noisy = noisy)
```

```{r targeting-map, fig.height=6.5}
plot_fishery(fished, "trawl", which_year = 2005, which_sim = NULL) |> vignette_widget()
```

The map counts every operation, including unsuccessful operations, pooled over
replicates. The adjoining panels compare true catch composition with unweighted
biological observations. Replace `fished` with `uniform` or `noisy` to inspect
the alternative location patterns. Annual quantities can be plotted directly:

```{r fishery-trends, fig.height=4.5}
plot_fishery_trend(fished, "trawl", metric = "n") |> vignette_widget()
```

### A five-year example: CPUE and true abundance

Preferential fishing means selecting locations according to fish density. It
differs from preferential monitoring of already completed operations. Here we
isolate fishing locations, holding gear, effort, and monitoring fixed.

We reuse the five-year `population` above, including its default shifting spatial
distribution. Equal selectivity at all ages removes changing age composition as
a cause of changing catchability. Both fishing scenarios have imperfect knowledge
(`knowledge_sd = 1`): map-error SD equals the year's initial mean vulnerable
density across accessible cells. Uniform fishing ignores this signal; targeted
fishing favors its higher values, with the default 5% exploration. The knowledge
setting is illustrative, not calibrated to a particular fleet.

The densest cell and concentration change without specifying a persistent core:

```{r cpue-distribution}
distribution <- population$sp_N[, list(N = sum(N)), by = c("year", "cell")]
distribution[, share := N / sum(N), by = "year"]
spatial_summary <- distribution[, list(
  peak_cell = cell[which.max(N)], peak_share = round(max(share), 2),
  effective_cells = round(1 / sum(share^2), 1)), by = "year"]
knitr::kable(spatial_summary)
```

`effective_cells` describes spatial spread: one means all fish are in one cell;
196 means an equal distribution over this grid. This is a summary of annual
densities, without tracking individual fish movements.

```{r cpue-fishing}
run_cpue <- function(targeting) {
  set.seed(602)
  sim_fishery(population,
    fishery_share = 0.2, catch_model = sim_capture(q = 1),
    selectivity = function(age) 1, targeting = targeting, knowledge_sd = 1,
    max_operations = 30, sampling_coverage = 0, n_sims = 5)
}
cpue_scenarios <- list(Uniform = run_cpue(0), Targeted = run_cpue(1))
for (result in cpue_scenarios) {
  stopifnot(all(result$fishery$annual$n_operations == 30),
            all(result$fishery$annual$status == "operation_limit"),
            !any(result$fishery$setdet$quota_limited),
            !any(result$fishery$setdet$mortality_limited))
}
```

Each year has 30 unit-effort operations, ending before the allocation is caught.
These runs intentionally have shortfalls. The checks rule out quota and mortality
capping as explanations for the CPUE pattern. Capture `q = 1` and the 400-square-kilometre
cell area give a low encounter probability; monitoring is disabled in both runs.
Default exploration is unchanged. A new noisy map is drawn each year in each
replicate; harvesters do not continue targeting last year's locations by default.

```{r cpue-summary}
cpue_summary <- data.table::rbindlist(lapply(names(cpue_scenarios), function(label) {
  result <- cpue_scenarios[[label]]
  summary <- result$fishery$annual[, list(cpue = sum(n) / sum(effort)), by = "year"]
  summary$scenario <- label
  summary$N <- colSums(result$N)[match(summary$year, result$years)]
  summary$relative_cpue <- summary$cpue / summary$cpue[1]
  summary$relative_N <- summary$N / summary$N[1]
  summary
}))
knitr::kable(cpue_summary[year %in% c(2001, 2005),
  list(scenario, year, N = round(N), CPUE = round(cpue, 1))])
```

```{r cpue-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5}
abundance <- cpue_summary[scenario == "Uniform", ]
trajectory <- plotly::plot_ly(x = abundance$year, y = abundance$relative_N,
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Abundance", legendgroup = "N",
  line = list(color = "black"), marker = list(color = "black", size = 6)) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Year"), yaxis = list(title = "Relative abundance / CPUE"))
proportionality <- plotly::plot_ly(x = c(0, 1.1), y = c(0, 1.1),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Proportional", line = list(color = "grey50", dash = "dash")) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Relative abundance"), yaxis = list(title = "Relative CPUE"))
colours <- c(Uniform = "#0072B2", Targeted = "#D55E00")
for (label in names(cpue_scenarios)) {
  keep <- cpue_summary$scenario == label
  values <- cpue_summary[keep, ]
  trajectory <- trajectory |> plotly::add_trace(x = values$year, y = values$relative_cpue,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = label, legendgroup = label,
    line = list(color = colours[[label]]), marker = list(color = colours[[label]], size = 6),
    inherit = FALSE)
  proportionality <- proportionality |> plotly::add_trace(x = values$relative_N, y = values$relative_cpue,
    text = paste0("Year: ", values$year, "<br>N: ", round(values$N), "<br>CPUE: ", round(values$cpue, 1)),
    hoverinfo = "text", type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = label,
    legendgroup = label, showlegend = FALSE, line = list(color = colours[[label]]),
    marker = list(color = colours[[label]], size = 6), inherit = FALSE)
}
plotly::subplot(trajectory, proportionality, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.25)) |> vignette_widget()
```

Values are normalized to each series' first-year mean. CPUE is total true catch
divided by total effort across five replicates conditional on this one population.
Targeted fishing achieves higher **absolute** CPUE than uniform fishing in this
run, despite imperfect knowledge. Its relative trajectory also responds to
changing spatial concentration and the noisy density signal. Neither realized
curve follows abundance exactly. Uniform fishing is proportional to abundance
in expectation before depletion, but 30 operations over a patchy 196-cell grid
produce appreciable sampling variation. Normalizing the series hides their
initial difference in absolute catch rates.

Preferential fishing does not always produce hyperstability. Changing spatial
concentration can make targeted CPUE decline more slowly **or more quickly**
than abundance. Simply moving an otherwise unchanged spatial pattern need not
break proportionality if harvesters can follow it. Noisy knowledge can reduce
that ability; its effects vary among realizations. The appendix gives the
location-weighted expectation. Five years illustrate these mechanisms without
fitting a CPUE standardization model, calibrating a real fleet, or treating
conditional replicate variability as empirical uncertainty.

Interpret these comparisons within the fixed-removals framework. More effort
does not independently increase the annual catch budget. It can change the
number and allocation of operations needed to approach that budget. Capacity,
depletion, available mortality, and quota capping can all affect CPUE.

The final operation keeps its specified effort when catch is capped by the
remaining target (`quota_limited`). Its CPUE is consequently quota-limited.
Annual CPUE is total catch divided by total effort, not an average of operation
ratios. Keep zero-catch operations and fishery identifiers, and compare effort
units carefully: matching placeholder labels do not make different gears'
effort comparable. Statistical CPUE standardization is left to downstream work.

Sharing a seed makes a scenario reproducible, but
changed operation sequences do not guarantee paired random innovations.

## How does monitoring change the available data?

Default reporting is unbiased and noiseless. Every operation is selected for
biological monitoring, up to the default length and age caps. We first reduce
coverage, then change preferential selection at that **same** coverage. A separate
scenario changes reporting while retaining default coverage.

```{r monitoring-comparisons}
random_monitoring <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl, list(sampling_coverage = 0.25)))
preferential_monitoring <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl,
  list(sampling_coverage = 0.25, sampling_targeting = 2)))
under_reporting <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl,
  list(reporting_factor = 0.8, reporting_cv = 0.2)))

for (result in list(random_monitoring, preferential_monitoring, under_reporting)) {
  stopifnot(identical(fished$fishery$catch_at_length, result$fishery$catch_at_length),
            identical(fished$fishery$mortality_ledger, result$fishery$mortality_ledger))
}
```

`reporting_factor` and `reporting_cv` specify the mean and coefficient of
variation of an operation-level lognormal multiplier. The same multiplier
applies to numbers and kilograms. Zero catches stay zero. Biological samples
come from actual catches, regardless of reported totals.

Coverage is an **expected** proportion, not a fixed count of selected operations.
Positive `sampling_targeting` favors larger reported catches. Its probabilities
are calibrated to the requested expected coverage. Fisheries retain operation,
length, and conditional age-sampling probabilities in their biological records.

```{r monitoring-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5}
annual <- under_reporting$fishery$annual[under_reporting$fishery$annual$fishery == "trawl", ]
limits <- range(c(annual$n, annual$reported_n)) / 1000
reporting <- plotly::plot_ly(x = annual$n / 1000, y = annual$reported_n / 1000,
  type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = "Reports", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  plotly::add_lines(x = limits, y = limits, inherit = FALSE, name = "Identity",
    line = list(color = "grey50", dash = "dash"), showlegend = FALSE) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "True catch (1000 fish)"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Reported catch (1000 fish)"))
truth <- fished$fishery$catch_at_length
truth <- truth[truth$fishery == "trawl", list(n = sum(n)), by = "length"]
truth <- truth[order(truth$length), ]
measured_frequency <- function(result) {
  sample <- result$fishery$samp
  count <- table(factor(sample$length[sample$fishery == "trawl"], levels = truth$length))
  as.numeric(count / sum(count))
}
composition <- plotly::plot_ly(x = truth$length, y = truth$n / sum(truth$n),
  type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Catch truth", line = list(color = "black")) |>
  plotly::add_lines(y = measured_frequency(random_monitoring), name = "Uniform monitoring",
    line = list(color = "#0072B2", dash = "dash")) |>
  plotly::add_lines(y = measured_frequency(preferential_monitoring), name = "Preferential monitoring",
    line = list(color = "#D55E00", dash = "dot")) |>
  plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Length group (cm)"), yaxis = list(title = "Proportion"))
plotly::subplot(reporting, composition, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.25)) |> vignette_widget()
```

Left: reporting errors and the identity line. Right: pooled catch truth and
unweighted length compositions from uniformly or preferentially monitored
operations, both at 25% expected coverage. These sample proportions are descriptive,
not design-weighted catch estimates.

Even uniformly selected operations with fixed fish-sampling caps do not produce
an automatically representative unweighted sample of all caught fish. Operations
with different catches can contribute similar numbers of measured fish. Known
unequal probabilities can support appropriate design-based weighting, but do
not by themselves correct spatial fishing preferences or gear selectivity when
inferring population abundance. Zero coverage creates a different limitation.

### Determine maturity for measured or aged fish

The default `maturity_sampling = "aged"` examines every aged fish. `"measured"`
examines every length-measured fish, and `"none"` disables maturity observations.
These options apply to both fisheries and surveys, with no additional maturity cap.

```{r maturity-observations}
measured_maturity <- run_fleets(modifyList(trawl, list(maturity_sampling = "measured")))
aged_sample <- fished$fishery$samp
measured_sample <- measured_maturity$fishery$samp
stopifnot(identical(aged_sample$sample, measured_sample$sample),
          identical(aged_sample$mature[aged_sample$maturity_observed],
                    measured_sample$mature[aged_sample$maturity_observed]))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  protocol = c("Aged", "Measured"),
  trawl_maturity_observations = c(
    sum(aged_sample$maturity_observed[aged_sample$fishery == "trawl"]),
    sum(measured_sample$maturity_observed[measured_sample$fishery == "trawl"]))
))
```

`mature` is a binary observation; unexamined fish have `NA`, not zero.
`maturity_observed` marks examinations and `n_maturity` counts them in summaries.
Latent states are drawn once for all measured fish after existing reporting and
length/age sampling. The protocol then masks observations. This preserves
existing samples and overlapping maturity states when only the protocol changes.
With `light = FALSE`, `sample_truth` retains latent states for inspection.

Biological maturation is stochastic here, but classification is perfect.
Misclassification, sex-specific maturation, and persistent individual histories
are outside the model. Also note the grouping distinction: fishery stratified
age caps apply per operation and length group; survey stratified caps apply at
the configured `age_space_group`, per replicate/year and length group.

## Independent survey programs

Configure surveys without `sim`, then execute them together on the same
five-year population. As in the `sim_survey()` example, survey allocation, gear
dimensions, and biological sample sizes use their defaults. This grid gives
**160 sets per year and replicate**, stratified by depth and location, each in
a different cell. The second program changes only the catchability curve and
its age/length basis.

```{r surveys}
set.seed(503)
programs <- fished |>
  sim_surveys(
    survey_A = sim_survey(),
    survey_B = sim_survey(q = sim_logistic(x50 = 40), q_by = "length")
  )
selected <- programs |> select_survey("survey_B") |> run_strat() |> strat_error()
head(selected$total_strat_error)
```

Both programs observe the same original rounded annual snapshot, including when
called after fisheries. Survey catches do not consume mortality budgets or
deplete another survey. All programs' locations and catches precede biological
subsampling; all existing subsampling precedes maturity observations.

Common population data, including `B` and `S`, are stored once. Program-specific
availability, sets, samples, summaries, and configurations live in
`survey_programs`. `select_survey()` restores the chosen program's observations
and spatial availability and clears incompatible cached analyses. The `surveys`
table used by `test_surveys()` remains a separate table of scenario designs.

```{r survey-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5}
survey_figures <- lapply(names(programs$survey_programs), function(label) {
  view <- programs |> select_survey(label) |> run_strat() |> strat_error()
  estimate <- view$total_strat_error
  plotly::plot_ly(x = estimate$year, y = estimate$I_hat / 1e6,
    type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = paste(label, "estimates")) |>
    plotly::add_lines(x = view$years, y = colSums(view$I) / 1e6, inherit = FALSE,
      name = paste(label, "availability"), line = list(color = "black")) |>
    plotly::layout(xaxis = list(title = "Year"), yaxis = list(title = "Available fish (millions)"))
})
plotly::subplot(survey_figures, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.09) |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.25)) |> vignette_widget()
```

Each program's estimates are compared with its own availability truth. The five
conditional replicates illustrate variability rather than establish precision. Existing survey graphics also work on extracted views:

```{r survey-view, fig.height=6.5}
plot_survey(selected, which_year = 2005, which_sim = 1) |> vignette_widget()
```

Survey counts now have corresponding catch weights:

```{r survey-catch-weights}
knitr::kable(head(selected$setdet[, list(sim, year, set, n, kg = round(kg, 3))]))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(sum(selected$setdet$kg), sum(selected$samp$weight))),
          isTRUE(all.equal(sum(selected$samp_totals$kg_caught), sum(selected$samp$weight))))
```

`samp$weight` is deterministic kilograms for every simulated caught fish, and
`full_setdet$kg` retains set/age totals when `light = FALSE`. Catch totals use all
fish, not the length subsample. Individual weights for unmeasured fish are latent
truth, not additional weight measurements. No weight measurement error is imposed.

The target of these existing analyses is **availability `I`, not total abundance
`N`**. Programs with different catchabilities need not have matching indices.
Adding `B` and `S` truth does not add biomass or mature-biomass estimators to
`run_strat()`.

Survey `samp` tables retain simulated fish with `measured` and `aged` flags.
Extract measured lengths with `samp[samp$measured, ]` and observed ages with
`samp[samp$aged, ]`; otherwise latent age information could enter an analysis.
Use `maturity_observed` for maturity observations. Fishery `samp` already contains
only measured fish, with missing unobserved ages. Add the program name before
combining survey tables: set identifiers are program-scoped.

The inherited `replicates` here are five fishing/observation replicates conditional
on one population trajectory. Matching identifiers do not identify the same
individual fish or shared length-stock draws across surveys and fisheries.
For independent biological histories, choose the recruitment, mortality, and
spatial process settings and regenerate abundance and distribution in an outer
simulation loop. Record seeds, settings, and package versions for
reproducibility. Canonical name ordering makes registration order irrelevant;
adding or renaming programs can still change random draws.

### Limits and extensions

Use these mechanisms to explore sampling and observation processes before
choosing downstream estimators. Discards, vessel routes, explicit trip/port
hierarchies, seasons, and population feedback are not represented. All simulated
fishery catches are retained. Reports can be fractional estimates, while true
commercial catches remain whole fish. Retain unsuccessful operations and
distinguish genuine zeros from missing data in downstream work.

Custom capture functions receive aggregate remaining age-length counts,
selectivity, cell area, and an operation record. They return whole-fish proposals
bounded by available counts, with zero proposals at zero selectivity. This
extension point permits alternative encounter/capacity responses without a
mechanistic implementation of every fishing gear.

## Backwards compatibility

For an older distributed simulation, attach the new relationships explicitly:

```{r migration, eval=FALSE}
sim$sim_weight <- sim_weight()
sim$sim_maturity <- sim_maturity()
sim$maturity_by <- "length"
sim <- round_sim(sim)
```

This refreshes mass summaries using existing cell rounding without regenerating
the trajectory. For an older abundance-only object, attach the same relationships
before its usual `sim_distribution()` call instead.
For number-only surveys of an older object, `maturity_sampling = "none"` permits
sampling without inventing missing biological models. The former fishery-level
`weight` arguments have been removed. Prefer `x50` to the deprecated `x0` name;
positional logistic calls and the default curve are preserved.

For number-only legacy objects, individual weights and positive-catch kilograms
are missing; empty catches have zero kilograms.

The fishery reference column `total_deaths` replaces the less explicit name
`death_budget`. Both names currently contain identical values for compatibility.
These are shared all-cause age/year deaths, repeated on each fishery's row,
rather than separate fishery allocations.

Multi-year fishery results created before the annual-stock selection correction
pooled population rows across years. Rerun those fisheries from their saved
populations, with the intended seeds and configurations; do not patch the old
ledger or regenerate the population trajectory. Calling `sim_fisheries()` again
replaces its fishery results from the original annual snapshots.

## Appendix A: mathematics of the extensions

The population-generation and stratified-estimation equations are described in
the original paper. This appendix takes the generated abundance, mortality,
length-age key, and grid as inputs and specifies the new mechanisms.

### Notation and units

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| \(a,l,y,c,f,r,j\) | Age, length group, year, cell, fishery, replicate, operation |
| \(N_{a,y}, n_{c,a,l}^{(j)}\) | Rounded annual abundance and remaining integer stock |
| \(P_{l,a}=P(l\mid a)\) | Growth-model length-age probabilities; columns sum to one |
| \(w_l,m_{a,l}\) | Kilograms per fish and maturity probability |
| \(p_{f,y},s_{f,a,l}\) | Fishery share and selectivity probabilities |
| \(A_c,G_j,T_j,E_j\) | Cell area, gear amount, duration, and nominal effort \(G_jT_j\) |
| \(q_f,q_{s,l}\) | Capture area per gear-time, and dimensionless survey catchability |
| \(\beta_f,\sigma_f,\epsilon_f\) | Targeting, knowledge-error multiplier, exploration |
| \(\pi_j,\pi_{L\mid j},\pi_{A\mid L,j}\) | Operation and conditional biological selection probabilities |

Indices omitted below are held fixed. The biological relationships are
deterministic probability/mean functions, constant across cells and years in
this milestone. Length-based population summaries evaluate them on the growth
key's discrete labels. Survey age-based length draws retain their historical
rounded-length path, so integration over length groups is a discretization of
that underlying relationship.

### A1. Weight, maturity, biomass, and mature biomass

The default functions are

\[
w_l=\alpha l^b,\quad \alpha=10^{-5.2106},\quad b=3.0879,
\qquad m(x)=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\{k(x-x_{50})\}.
\]

Weight uses centimetres and kilograms. Default maturity uses \(k=0.28\)
per centimetre and \(x_{50}=47.81\) cm. For length-based maturity,
\(m_{a,l}=m(l)\); for age-based maturity, \(m_{a,l}=m(a)\).

\[
B_{a,y}=N_{a,y}\sum_lP_{l,a}w_l,\qquad
S_{a,y}=N_{a,y}\sum_lP_{l,a}w_lm_{a,l},
\]
\[
B_{l,y}=w_l\sum_aN_{a,y}P_{l,a},\qquad
S_{l,y}=w_l\sum_aN_{a,y}P_{l,a}m_{a,l}.
\]

These equations give equal annual totals across age and length representations,
with \(0\le S\le B\). Spatial values multiply cell abundance at age by the same
conditional expectations. All summaries are refreshed after rounding changes
abundance. No mortality timing, female fraction, or fecundity adjustment is applied.

As a hand calculation, suppose an age group contains 100 fish, with probabilities
0.75 and 0.25 of lengths whose weights are 1 and 8 kg and maturities 0 and 1.
Biomass is \(100(0.75+0.25\times8)=275\) kg; mature biomass is
\(100(0.25\times8)=200\) kg. Multiplying biomass by mean maturity instead gives
only \(275\times0.25=68.75\) kg. Converting an age-based mass matrix with the
ordinary number-based length-age key would likewise lose the relevant association.

### A2. Reference catches and integer mortality budgets

Mean selectivity at age and reference fishing mortality are

\[
\bar s_{f,a}=\sum_lP_{l,a}s_{f,a,l},\qquad
F^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}=p_{f,y}Z_{a,y}\bar s_{f,a}.
\]

For constant annual mortality, the
[Baranov reference catch](https://www.fao.org/4/X9026E/x9026e06.htm) becomes

\[
C^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}
=N_{a,y}\frac{F^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}}{Z_{a,y}}(1-e^{-Z_{a,y}})
=N_{a,y}p_{f,y}\bar s_{f,a}(1-e^{-Z_{a,y}}).
\]

The final expression defines zero catch at \(Z=0\), without division by zero.
The constraint is \(\sum_f p_{f,y}\bar s_{f,a}\le1\) for every age/year
(up to floating-point tolerance). These are reference quantities: realized age
composition and implied allocation of deaths may differ.

Cell abundances are rounded with R's `round()` convention and annual abundance
is recomputed from cells. Within each cell/age, integer length stocks are drawn
as a multinomial allocation of that cell count with probabilities \(P_{l,a}\).
They are independent allocations in each replicate/year, not tracked individuals.

Define balanced rounding \(\mathcal R(\mathbf x)\) by flooring each value and
adding one to the largest fractional remainders until the total is
`round(sum(x))`. R uses ties-to-even for half-integer totals; remainder ties use
age order or canonical fishery-name order. Then

\[
\mathbf D_y=\mathcal R\{N_{a,y}(1-e^{-Z_{a,y}})\}_a,\qquad
\mathbf Q_y=\mathcal R\{\sum_a C^{\mathrm{ref}}_{f,a,y}\}_f.
\]

\(D_{a,y}\), stored as `total_deaths`, is the shared whole-fish count of all
deaths at age, including fishing and other deaths. \(Q_{f,y}\) is one fishery's
total-number target. Target rounding is joint across fisheries, not independent rounding
of each age/fishery catch. The valid combined target cannot exceed the overall
death budget; realized catches must additionally fit age-specific budgets.

After fishing, retain true catches and their mortality equivalents at age:

\[
U^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}=\frac{C^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}}{N_{a,y}},\qquad
F^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}=U^{\mathrm{realized}}_{f,a,y}
\frac{Z_{a,y}}{1-e^{-Z_{a,y}}}.
\]

For positive N and zero Z, realized catches and F are zero. At zero N, both
realized rates are missing. The factor uses `-expm1(-Z)` for numerical stability.
No operation-time hazard is fitted and no future abundance is changed. Integer
rounding can give a death budget above the continuous expectation, so combined
equivalent F may exceed Z in tiny populations; values are retained without clipping.
The stored N, Z, and integer budget allow the discrepancy to be inspected.

### A3. Location probabilities and knowledge errors

Within a replicate/year, initial vulnerable density defines a persistent map
error for each fishery/cell. On accessible cells, let

\[
d^{(0)}_{f,c}=A_c^{-1}\sum_{a,l}n^{(0)}_{c,a,l}s_{f,a,l},\qquad
e_{f,c}\sim N\{0,(\sigma_f\overline d^{(0)}_f)^2\}.
\]

Errors are drawn once and reused across operations, with the mean taken over
accessible cells. Current density excludes ages with exhausted death budgets:

\[
d^{(j)}_{f,c}=A_c^{-1}\sum_{a,l}n^{(j)}_{c,a,l}s_{f,a,l}
\mathbf1(D^{\mathrm{remaining}}_a>0),\qquad
u^{(j)}_{f,c}=\max(0,d^{(j)}_{f,c}+e_{f,c})^{\beta_f}.
\]

For \(K_f\) accessible cells, the location probability is

\[
P(c\mid f,j)=(1-\epsilon_f)
\frac{u^{(j)}_{f,c}}{\sum_{c'}u^{(j)}_{f,c'}}+\frac{\epsilon_f}{K_f}.
\]

Zero targeting or an all-zero signal gives uniform probabilities. All accessible
cells remain in this location frame, including cells that can produce zero
catches. A fishery is exhausted when no accessible vulnerable stock has remaining
age mortality, even though the signal may suggest otherwise. Noisy knowledge
with zero targeting does not change the uniform choice probabilities.

### A4. Capture proposals, thinning, and interleaving

For a selected cell, the built-in proposal probability and counts are

\[
v_{a,l,j}=1-\exp\left(-q_fG_jT_js_{f,a,l}/A_c\right),\qquad
X_{a,l,j}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n^{(j)}_{c,a,l},v_{a,l,j}).
\]

The engine thins proposals without replacement, first for capacity
\(\lfloor\texttt{capacity\_per\_gear}\,G_j\rfloor\), then within each age for
remaining mortality, and finally across accepted proposals for the remaining
fishery target. With category counts \(\mathbf x\), thinning to \(h\) fish uses
the multivariate hypergeometric distribution; counts are not expanded into fish.
Accepted catches reduce the common stock and age death budgets.

The capture probability describes a proposal, not the final constrained catch
distribution. `mortality_limited` and `quota_limited` flag their respective
constraints. All specified \(E_j=G_jT_j\) remains when the quota caps a catch.

One replicate/year follows this algorithm:

1. Initialize stocks, death budgets, and every fishery target once.
2. Choose the next active fishery uniformly; check its opportunities and operation limit.
3. Choose a location, resolve gear/time, propose catches, and apply constraints.
4. Update shared stock/budgets and retain the operation, including a zero catch.
5. Retire completed/exhausted/limited fisheries and repeat until none is active.
6. Allocate other deaths, then complete reporting and biological samples.

The known impossible built-in cases (`q = 0` or zero capacity) retire as exhausted.
A custom model returning zeros can instead reach its operation limit, because
the engine cannot infer all future responses of an arbitrary callback.

### A5. Residual mortality and conservation

After fishing, residual deaths at age are

\[
O_a=D_a-\sum_{f,c,l}C_{f,c,a,l}.
\]

Sample those deaths without replacement among all remaining fish at that age,
across cells and lengths. For every ledger row,

\[
n^{(0)}_{c,a,l}=\sum_f C_{f,c,a,l}+O_{c,a,l}+V_{c,a,l},
\]

where \(V\) denotes survivors. Integer stocks balance exactly. Population `B`
and `S` integrate over the length key, whereas each fishery replicate has a
particular integer length allocation; their starting masses need not be identical.
None of these deaths is subtracted again from a future pre-generated population.

### A6. Reporting and preferential monitoring

For mean reporting factor \(b\) and CV \(c\), draw independent operation multipliers

\[
\sigma_R^2=\log(1+c^2),\qquad
\log R_j\sim N(\log b-\sigma_R^2/2,\sigma_R^2).
\]

Thus \(E(R_j)=b\). Reported numbers and kilograms equal their true values times
the same \(R_j\). At zero CV the multiplier is constant; at zero mean it is zero.

Within each fishery/replicate/year, operation weights use reported catch \(r_j\):

\[
w_j=(1+r_j/\overline r)^\gamma,\qquad
\pi_j=\min(1,\lambda w_j),\qquad
\sum_j\pi_j=\texttt{sampling\_coverage}\times J.
\]

\(\gamma\) is `sampling_targeting`. Zero targeting or all-zero reported catches
gives equal probabilities. Selection is independent Bernoulli with these
probabilities, so realized coverage varies. The implementation rescales weights
for numerical stability and retains a positive numerical floor under extreme
preferences. Coverage zero and one are handled directly.

For a selected operation with catch \(C_j\), measure
\(n_{L,j}=\min(C_j,\texttt{lengths\_cap})\) fish without replacement. The
conditional length-selection probability is \(n_{L,j}/C_j\). Random age sampling
selects up to `ages_cap` from these fish. Stratified sampling selects up to that
cap within each measured length group, per operation. The conditional probability
within an age-sampling group is its selected count divided by its measured count.
Zero coverage or caps disable the corresponding observations.

Recorded probabilities describe the stages conditional on the realized frame
and previous sample. Their product is a multistage selection factor; it is not
automatically the unconditional marginal inclusion probability when later groups
depend on earlier random samples. Appropriate inference also needs a defined
estimand, frame, and positive coverage. No catch-composition estimator is supplied
by this vignette.

### A7. Maturity observations

After every existing sample is generated, draw a latent state for each measured
fish \(i\):

\[
M_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\{m(x_i)\},\qquad
x_i=l_i\ \text{or}\ a_i.
\]

Use the simulated true age internally when maturity depends on age, even if it
will not be observed. The observation indicator is `aged`, `measured`, or zero
according to `maturity_sampling`. Report \(M_i\) when examined and `NA` otherwise.
Latent draws occur even for `"none"` when a model is present, so protocol changes
preserve overlapping states and RNG consumption. Only the bounded measured
sample is materialized for fisheries; no individual commercial-population
maturity records are needed to calculate expected `S`.

### A8. Length-selective survey observations

For length catchability \(q_{s,l}\), program-specific availability is

\[
\overline q_{s,a}=\sum_lP_{l,a}q_{s,l},\qquad
I_{s,a,y}=N_{a,y}\overline q_{s,a},\qquad
I_{s,l,y}=q_{s,l}\sum_aN_{a,y}P_{l,a}.
\]

Caught lengths conditional on age follow
\(P(l\mid a,\text{caught},s)=P_{l,a}q_{s,l}/\overline q_{s,a}\).
At zero availability there is no catch, so that conditional distribution is
never sampled. The historical age-based path uses age catchability and the
original growth sampler. New length-based draws use the growth key's labels.

Survey catches at age use binomial trials with rounded cell abundance divided
by the number of sets in that cell, and probability
\((A_{\mathrm{tow}}/A_c)\overline q_{s,a}\). Repeated-cell handling retains that
historical splitting convention; it is not fishery-style sequential depletion.
`binom_error = FALSE` rounds the corresponding expectation. Swept-area and
catchability settings must define valid probabilities. Length caps apply per
set; stratified survey age caps use `age_space_group` per replicate/year/length
group, while random caps apply per set.

For every realized caught fish i, deterministic weight is \(w(l_i)\). Catch mass
for set j is \(K_j=\sum_{i\in j}w(l_i)\), including unmeasured fish; set/age and
replicate/year totals sum the same realized weights. These are not population
biomass expectations or estimates scaled from the measured subsample. Legacy
objects without a weight model retain missing individual weights and nonempty
catch masses, with mass zero for an empty catch.

### A9. Biomass catches, CPUE, and random sequencing

With realized joint catches \(C_{j,a,l}\), operation biomass is
\(K_j=\sum_{a,l}C_{j,a,l}w_l\). Population weights apply to every fishery.
For a fishery/replicate/year,

\[
\operatorname{CPUE}=\frac{\sum_j C_j}{\sum_j E_j},\qquad
\operatorname{CPUE}_{\mathrm{biomass}}=\frac{\sum_j K_j}{\sum_j E_j}.
\]

Reported versions use reported totals. Zero total effort gives missing CPUE;
zero catches with positive effort give zero CPUE. Biomass is stored in kilograms,
even when figures display tonnes. Different fisheries' effort is not pooled.

All fisheries' truth across replicates/years is generated before reporting and
biological sampling. Survey programs likewise generate all their truth before
biological subsampling. Maturity follows every existing sample in its batch.
Names are processed canonically, and all draws use the caller's RNG state.
Changing earlier pipeline stages can still change later stages' RNG state;
repeat a stage from an explicit seed when constructing controlled comparisons.


### A10. Spatial preferences and CPUE proportionality

Consider the five-year example's equal-area cells, full selectivity, constant
effort E, and inactive capacity/quota/mortality constraints. Before depletion,
let \(n_c\) be abundance in cell c and \(N=\sum_c n_c\). With constant encounter
probability \(v=1-\exp(-q_fE/A_c)\), expected first-operation CPUE is

\[
E(C/E)=\frac{v}{E}\sum_c\pi_c n_c.
\]

Uniform fishing in K accessible cells gives \(vN/(EK)\). In the special case
of accurate density targeting with exploration \(\epsilon\), the expectation is

\[
E(C/E)=\frac{v}{E}\left\{(1-\epsilon)\frac{\sum_c n_c^2}{N}
+\epsilon\frac{N}{K}\right\}.
\]

With imperfect knowledge, let \(h_c=\max(0,n_c/A_c+e_c)\), using the
replicate/year's errors from A3. For positive total signal and `targeting = 1`,

\[
E(C/E\mid\mathbf e)=\frac{v}{E}\left\{(1-\epsilon)
\frac{\sum_c n_ch_c}{\sum_c h_c}+\epsilon\frac{N}{K}\right\}.
\]

An all-zero signal uses uniform probabilities. The example uses this noisy
signal with `knowledge_sd = 1`, not the accurate-knowledge special case. New
errors are drawn around each year's distribution; within-year density updates
after catches, while those errors stay fixed. There is no dependence on the
previous year's fishing map.

If \(n_c=Nr_c\) with constant relative spatial proportions \(r_c\),
accurate-targeting and uniform expectations are proportional to N. Permuting
cells does not change those expectations. Since error SD scales with initial
mean density, a proportionally scaled population also has a proportionally
scaled noisy signal distribution, before depletion. Movement alone therefore
does not necessarily break proportionality under this contemporaneous model.
Changing concentration or knowledge quality can change the location-weighted
density factor in either direction. The example uses the default stochastic
processes for abundance and spatial structure, so neither a monotonic decline
nor a particular direction of CPUE departure is imposed.

Annual simulated CPUE also reflects finite operations and within-year depletion;
the first-operation equation explains the mechanism, not an exact annual fit.
The example checks that quota and mortality capping are inactive and uses the
same annual effort for both strategies. It does not prescribe a particular
CPUE-abundance relationship or imply empirical uncertainty from these replicates.
